## Research question

Do young Americans pursue further education in response to deteriorating
labour market conditions in the US since 2000?

The intuition is simple. The opportunity cost of going back to school is
the wage you would otherwise earn. When the labour market is weak,
graduates have a more difficult time finding an entry-level job that
suits their preferences. A weak labour market is often characterised by
a high unemployment rate and/or low wage offers, among other factors.
This circumstance leads many students to pursue further education in
hopes of better times (staying in school longer has relatively lower
opportunity costs). We test this hypothesis using master’s enrolment,
the most common form of further education for students who already hold
a bachelor’s degree.

## Data

Our database holds nine series for the US since 2000:

-   **Eight monthly series from FRED**: unemployment rate (`UNRATE`),
    job-openings rate (`JTSJOR`), hires rate (`JTSHIL`), quits rate
    (`JTSQUR`), involuntary part-time work (`LNS12032194`), nonfarm
    payrolls (`PAYEMS`), the unemployment rate of
    bachelor's-degree-and-above (`LNS14027662`), and the NBER recession
    indicator (`USREC`).
-   **One annual series from NCES**: total postbaccalaureate fall
    enrollment in US degree-granting institutions
    (`MASTERS_ENROLLMENT`), 2000-2022, from the Digest of Education
    Statistics, Table 303.80.

The data lives in a DuckDB star schema (see @fig-er) built once by
`data/build_fred.py`. After the build, the database is the only data
source for this brief, every figure and table comes from
`LabourMarketFramework` in `src/labour_market_framework.py`.

![Database schema. One dimension table (`series`) holds the metadata,
one fact table (`observations`) holds the values.
`observations.series_id` references `series.series_id`, with
`(series_id, date)` as the composite primary key on the fact
table.](../data/star_schema_sketch.png){#fig-er}

## A first look at the data

@tbl-descriptive summarises every series.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-descriptive
#| tbl-cap: "Summary statistics for the nine series, full sample. Master's enrollment is annual (23 observations, 2000-2022), the others are monthly."
lmf.descriptive_stats()
```

Two numbers from this table provide context for the rest of the
analysis. UNRATE peaked at 14.8% in April 2020 and averaged 5.6% over
the sample. Master's enrollment grew from 2.16 million in 2000 to 3.21
million in 2022, a 47% rise in 22 years.

## The labour market since 2000

@fig-beveridge plots job openings against unemployment, the Beveridge
curve. A healthy market shows a downward slope: when unemployment falls,
vacancies rise, and the points sit on one curve. Outward shifts indicate
structural change.

```{python}
#| label: fig-beveridge
#| fig-cap: "US Beveridge curve, December 2000 to present. Points coloured by year; recession months ringed in red."
fig = lmf.plot_beveridge_curve()
```

Three patterns are visible. The 2001 and 2008-09 recessions show a move
down and to the right (more unemployment, fewer openings). The April
2020 point sits at the extreme bottom right (as mentioned before: 14.8%
unemployment, 3.4% openings). From 2021 onward the points lie above the
historical curve at the same unemployment level: same unemployment, more
openings than before.

## A composite stress index

UNRATE captures one dimension of the labour market. To test our research
question we want a broader approach, so we built our own **labour-market
stress index** using the `compute_stress_index` method on our class.

**How it is built.** Four monthly FRED series enter the index by
default: the quits rate (`JTSQUR`), the hires rate (`JTSHIL`),
involuntary part-time work (`LNS12032194`) and nonfarm payrolls
(`PAYEMS`). Each series is z-scored (mean 0, standard deviation 1) so
that scales do not distort our results. Signs are then applied so higher
values mean worse labour-market conditions: involuntary part-time work
gets +1 (more part-timers stuck part-time = worse), quits, hires, and
payrolls each get -1 (lower = worse). The four signed z-scores are
averaged into one number per month.

**Goal.** Summarise the labour-market state in a single, comparable
series so we can ask whether enrollment responds to the labour market
measured as our index, rather than to one indicator like UNRATE alone.

**Reading the index.** Zero is roughly average for 2000-present.
Positive readings mean conditions are worse than average, negative
readings mean better.

```{python}
#| label: fig-stress-alone
#| fig-cap: "Labour-market stress index, US December 2000 to present. Z-scored, higher means worse conditions. Recessions shaded."
stress = lmf.compute_stress_index()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
for ep_start, ep_end in lmf.tag_recession_episodes():
    ax.axvspan(ep_start, ep_end, color="lightgrey", alpha=0.4)
ax.plot(stress.index, stress.values, color="navy", linewidth=1.5)
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Stress index (z-score)")
ax.set_title("Labour-market stress index, US 2000-present")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout()
```

The index lines up with the three recessions of our sample. It rises
through the 2001 dot-com bust, peaks at the 2008-09 financial crisis,
and spikes sharply in April 2020 before falling back again. Since 2022 a
labour market is observed that, under historical comparison, is quite
tight.

## Enrollment and the stress index

@fig-stress-vs-enrollment puts the index next to the yearly growth of
master's enrollment. The left axis is the index (higher = worse), the
right axis is enrollment growth.

```{python}
#| label: fig-stress-vs-enrollment
#| fig-cap: "Labour-market stress index (left axis, blue) and master's enrollment growth (right axis, red). Recessions shaded."
fig = lmf.plot_stress_index_vs_enrollment()
```

The 2001 and 2008-09 recessions match our intuition closely. The index
rises strongly during each recession, enrollment growth peaks roughly
one year later, at 6.5% in 2002 and 4.1% in 2009. The one-year lag is
explained by the length of the academic admission cycle: people who
decide to go back to school during a downturn show up in enrollment data
the next September.

The 2020 COVID-19 recession is the exception. The stress index peaked in
April 2020, but enrollment growth in 2021 was only 2.3% - weaker than
their responses to earlier recessions. A possible explanation could be
that the pandemic e.g. disrupted admissions and on-campus life. These
problems may have suppressed the effect that earlier recessions had on
the master's enrollment.

## Discussion

**The opportunity-cost intuition holds, with a 2020 exception.** For the
2001 and 2008-09 recessions, master's enrollment grew most when the
broader labour-market was worst (@fig-stress-vs-enrollment). The 2020
recession shows different results, that can be explained by e.g. closed
campuses and disrupted admissions.

**Limitations of our analysis.** Master's enrollment is annual and is
stored at January-1 of each year, while the FRED series are monthly. We
align the two using yearly growth, but the underlying admission
decisions happen already earlier, not on the first of January. Also,
master's enrollment is measured in absolute figures, therefore, one has
to take into account a growing US population (about 18% between 2000 and
2022) that partially explains growing master's enrollment numbers as
well. The NCES Digest has no 2023 figure yet, so the most recent
enrollment observation is fall 2022. The involuntary-part-time series
(`LNS12032194`) has one missing month at the very end of the sample,
visible as a slightly shorter `count` in @tbl-descriptive.

## Conclusion

Master's enrollment in the US has moved in line with labour-market
stress for most of the period since 2000. The relationship is clearest
for the 2001 and 2008-09 recessions, it does not hold for the 2020
COVID-19 episode, probably because other problems caused by the pandemic
held against the usual effect. The reusable Python class
`LabourMarketFramework` (see the User Guide) produced every figure and
table in this brief, the same toolkit can be repointed at a different
economy by swapping the DuckDB file.
